sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: The international system is undergoing a multilayered process of change in the first quarter of the twenty-first century, with economic, technological, and geopolitical transformations taking place simultaneously. China’s growing weight in global production, trade, finance, and technology ecosystems has also enabled Asia to become one of the principal centers of the global system. Rather than a linear shift of the axis in which one center simply replaces another, this trend points to a more plural order in which different centers of power are influential at the same time. The 55th anniversary (1971-2026) of diplomatic relations between the Republic of Türkiye and the People’s Republic of China provides a meaningful historical threshold for assessing how this systemic change is reflected in bilateral relations.

The trajectory of relations can be summarized through four turning points. Diplomatic relations were established on August 5, 1971; contacts diversified from the 1980s onward as both countries pursued policies of opening up; relations were elevated to the level of “strategic cooperation” in 2010; and in 2015 a memorandum was signed on harmonizing the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) with the Middle Corridor. Following the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine War in 2022, the rise in political and logistical risks along the Northern Corridor through Russia made the Middle Corridor, which runs across the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus, and Türkiye, more visible (Atlı, 2013; Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye, 2016; Ülgen & Umarov, 2024).

The literature on Türkiye-China relations reveals from different perspectives the tension between diplomatic rapprochement and economic asymmetry. Studies show that the discourse of strategic cooperation has not translated into a balanced partnership in trade and investment, that Türkiye seeks to expand its room for autonomy with China while maintaining its ties with Western institutions, and that the complementarity between the Middle Corridor and the BRI is conditional (Hussain, 2021; Öniş & Yalikun, 2021; Tekdal, 2024). However, studies that evaluate power transition, connectivity, the technological composition of trade, the quality of investment, and the peace-stability relationship within a single analytical model remain limited. This fragmentation in the literature makes it difficult to test explicitly under what conditions expanding trade and infrastructure investment generate productive capacity and balanced interdependence.

This article addresses the following question: Does Türkiye remain merely a “transit country” within Eurasian production and logistics networks integrated with China, or is it becoming a “joint production hub” through technology transfer, joint R&D, local value added, and reciprocal investment? The answer is not inferred from single indicators such as geographic location or total trade volume. Transit-country status is operationalized as a situation in which transport volume, travel time, and corridor capacity improve while production, technology, and local-supply linkages remain weak; joint-production-hub status, by contrast, requires foreign direct investment to make measurable contributions to manufacturing, R&D, local sourcing, and exports to third countries.

The study makes an original contribution at three levels. First, it examines the 55-year relationship by combining diplomatic periodization with geoeconomic indicators. Second, rather than treating the geopolitical importance of the Middle Corridor as an automatic economic success, it measures its transit and production functions separately. Third, it develops the “new peace perspective” not as an established theory, but as a conditional analytical framework that brings together the literatures on commercial peace, complex interdependence, and weaponized interdependence. In this way, official discourse on “common development” is separated from data-based analytical assessment.

sections.title: Theoretical Framework and Position in the Literature
paragraphs: The power-transition approach explains change in the international system not merely through the absolute growth of a single state, but through the different rates at which the relative economic, technological, and military capabilities of major actors develop. According to Gilpin (1981), shifts in the distribution of power alter the costs and benefits of existing rules and create pressure for systemic adjustment. China’s rise is important in this context; however, China’s economic size does not imply that a multipolar order will inevitably be peaceful or China-centered. Power transition creates competition over technology standards, finance, critical inputs, and transport networks as well as opportunities for cooperation. This study therefore treats China’s rise not as the normative proclamation of a “new paradigm,” but as a systemic variable that redistributes options and constraints across Eurasia.

Geoeconomics is the second theoretical component and explains how states use trade, finance, investment, technology, and infrastructure instruments to pursue strategic objectives. In Luttwak’s (1990) approach, the logic of competition persists while the instruments become increasingly economic. In this framework, a port, railway, or digital network is not merely technical infrastructure; it is a source of power that affects market access, costs, standards, and relations of dependence. Connectivity, in turn, refers to the capacity of these instruments to operate together within geographic, institutional, and digital networks. Corridor analysis must therefore encompass customs harmonization, financing conditions, data sharing, logistics services, and production clusters in addition to the physical route itself.

The interdependence literature explains the dual nature of connectivity as a source of both cooperation and vulnerability. According to Keohane and Nye (2012), economic and institutional networks generate mutual sensitivity and costs among actors, although these costs may be distributed unevenly. Farrell and Newman (2019) developed the concept of “weaponized interdependence” by showing how actors that control central network nodes can turn informational and access advantages into instruments of coercion. This perspective demonstrates why growth in trade volume alone should not be treated as an indicator of partnership. In Türkiye-China relations, the trade deficit, technological dependence, and the sectoral distribution of investment shape the distribution of bargaining power as much as the benefits of connectivity.

Although the literature on Türkiye-China relations addresses different dimensions of these theoretical debates, it generally concentrates on a single level of analysis. Atlı (2018) and Tekdal (2024) evaluate Ankara’s relations with China in the context of foreign-policy diversification and strategic autonomy, while Öniş and Yalikun (2021) emphasize the gap between political rapprochement and asymmetric economic outcomes. Işık and Zou (2019) examine security cooperation, while Hussain (2021) analyzes elements of complementarity and competition between the BRI and the Middle Corridor. Duan and Aydın (2024) show how the historical processes of state- and nation-building in the two countries affect bilateral relations. The present study does not reject these contributions; instead, it integrates them around productive capacity, logistics performance, and a conditional mechanism of stability.

The explanatory chain of the theoretical model is constructed as follows: shifts in the global distribution of power increase states’ efforts to exert influence through economic networks and corridors; geoeconomic investments create new connections while potentially distributing gains and vulnerabilities unevenly. For Türkiye, if logistics access is supported by production linkages, local value added, export capacity, and bargaining power may increase. If connectivity remains confined to a transit function and one-sided dependence deepens in critical technologies and inputs, economic networks may narrow Türkiye’s strategic room for maneuver. Balanced investment, joint institutions, and positive expectations about future cooperation, by contrast, may contribute to stability by increasing the cost of disputes.

This model generates three analytical expectations. First, if transport capacity expands while production-oriented investment and technology transfer remain low, Türkiye will occupy a predominantly transit-based position. Second, if foreign direct investment generates local sourcing, R&D, skilled employment, and exports to third countries, a transition toward a joint production hub can be identified. Third, if economic relations are markedly asymmetric, the pacifying effect of connectivity will be limited; its potential to generate stability will rise as reciprocity, institutionalization, and positive expectations that future cooperation will continue become stronger. The findings are interpreted on the basis of these expectations.

The model also draws a clear distinction among official discourse, policy outputs, and economic outcomes. Expressions such as “strategic cooperation,” “common development,” or “harmonization” indicate the parties’ intentions and the political framework they assign to the relationship; by themselves, they do not constitute evidence of complementarity, local development, or balanced interdependence. Policy outputs are observable steps such as signed memoranda, established working groups, or allocated financing. Economic outcomes are sought in realized indicators of freight volume, investment, local sourcing, R&D, and exports. Separating these three levels prevents normative expectations from being confused with realized outcomes and places the discourse-implementation gap in Türkiye-China relations at the center of the analysis.

sections.title: Method, Data Sources, and Analytical Criteria
paragraphs: The research is based on a structured qualitative document analysis covering the period 1971-2026. Document analysis requires written materials produced for different purposes to be systematically selected, evaluated, and interpreted under thematic categories (Bowen, 2009). This design was chosen because it allows the 55-year historical trajectory to be compared within the same framework as bilateral trade, investment, and transport indicators. The study does not perform statistical tests of causality; instead, it evaluates the fit between theoretical expectations and observed indicators through triangulation across sources.

The source universe consists of four groups. The first includes official documents concerning the establishment of diplomatic relations, the 2010 strategic cooperation decision, the 2015 harmonization memorandum, connectivity, and mediation activities. The second includes the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye’s bilateral trade series, World Bank Middle Corridor modeling and project-financing data, and investment announcements by the Investment Office of the Presidency of the Republic of Türkiye. The third group consists of peer-reviewed articles and academic books, and the fourth of data-based reports from research institutions such as the Carnegie Endowment and SWP. Official documents are used to identify actors’ policy goals and announced figures, while academic studies are used to assess these claims critically and comparatively.

Sources were selected according to direct relevance to the subject, institutional or academic reliability, traceability of the method by which data were produced, and temporal coverage. For trade data, Türkiye’s official series based on the general trade system was taken as the basis; different national series were not combined in the same table because mirror statistics from the Chinese side may differ. Future figures concerning the Middle Corridor were classified not as realized outcomes but as World Bank model projections conditional on investment and efficiency measures. Capacity, employment, and R&D information relating to the BYD investment was likewise coded as announced targets rather than realized technology transfer.

The analysis was conducted in three stages. In the first stage, documents were coded chronologically into the periods 1971-1989, 1990-2009, 2010-2021, and 2022-2026. In the second, the content was grouped under the themes of power transition, geoeconomic connectivity, trade-technological asymmetry, investment and production cooperation, political constraints, and the peace-stability mechanism. In the third stage, the research question was evaluated using the criteria in Table 1, and where possible the same claim was compared across official data, international-organization reports, and academic interpretation. This procedure reduces the risk of presenting official discourse on “common development” as an analytical finding.

During the coding process, the date, document type, institutional producer, period covered, principal claim, and indicator used were recorded for each document. Quantitative claims were divided into three categories: “realized data,” “announced target,” and “model projection.” Thus, the 2023 foreign-trade figures are realized data, the BYD facility’s capacity of 150,000 vehicles is an announced target, and the Middle Corridor reaching 11 million tonnes in 2030 is a conditional projection. Where sources differed, a comparable series within the same statistical system was preferred and alternative figures were not combined. Evidence running against the research question was retained alongside supportive findings; for this reason, the corridor’s limited share of China-Europe trade and the lack of data on technology transfer were not excluded.

The method has two limitations. First, regular and comparable open data are limited regarding local-sourcing ratios in Chinese investment, firm-level R&D expenditure, and bilateral patent production. The absence of data is therefore interpreted not as proof that no technology transfer occurs, but as evidence that the claim of a production hub cannot yet be verified with transparent indicators. Second, the World Bank’s 2030 corridor estimates are based on a broader regional model that includes Türkiye and cannot be used as precise country-level outcomes. These limitations are explicitly retained in the findings section.

sections.title: Historical Trajectory of Relations
paragraphs: The first period is the phase of cautious normalization extending from diplomatic recognition in 1971 to the end of the 1980s. Türkiye’s recognition of the People’s Republic of China was closely connected to Cold War conditions and the change in China’s representation at the United Nations. Bilateral relations were initially conducted through limited diplomatic contacts; in the 1980s, trade and official visits increased as economic opening accelerated in both countries (Atlı, 2013; Duan & Aydın, 2024). At this stage the relationship did not yet possess a strategic framework; its principal achievement was mutual recognition and the establishment of regular diplomatic contact.

The second period, from 1990 to 2009, was a phase in which economic relations expanded faster than political relations. The end of the Cold War, China’s integration into global production networks, and the greater opening of Türkiye’s market to foreign trade increased bilateral trade. Türkiye’s exports to China, however, did not diversify at the same pace, and the gap in favor of imports became persistent. This period established the structural pattern that would become more pronounced in subsequent years: despite growing political contacts and trade volume, Türkiye’s share of the Chinese market and China-origin production investment in Türkiye remained limited (Dilek et al., 2019; Öniş & Yalikun, 2021).

The third period began with the elevation of relations to the level of “strategic cooperation” in 2010 and acquired an institutional-connectivity dimension with the 2015 harmonization memorandum. The memorandum of November 14, 2015 provided a political and legal basis for cooperation on road, railway, and port connections between the BRI and the Middle Corridor (Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye, 2016). This development does not mean that every element of the two initiatives was automatically integrated. Route priorities, financing, technical standards, and local-development objectives involve a need for negotiation and coordination as well as complementarity (Hussain, 2021).

The fourth period, beginning after 2022, is characterized by the rising importance of geopolitical risks and supply-chain security. The Russia-Ukraine War and sanctions against Russia increased the risk premium of transport through the Northern Corridor, attracting greater attention to the Middle Corridor as an alternative and diversifying route. During the same period, U.S.-China technology competition and the European Union’s policies to reduce China-related economic risks made Türkiye’s room for maneuver more complex given its NATO membership and Customs Union with the EU. The 55-year relationship is therefore better characterized as a selective partnership in which diplomatic cooperation, economic asymmetry, and security constraints are managed together rather than as a linear process of rapprochement (Tekdal, 2024; Ülgen & Umarov, 2024).

This periodization reveals both continuity and change in the relationship. The continuity lies in Türkiye’s desire to diversify economic relations with China and to balance the trade deficit through investment, an objective maintained from before 2010 to the present. The change is visible in the instruments of the relationship: strategic cooperation was added to the initial agenda of diplomatic recognition and trade after 2010, corridor harmonization after 2015, and supply-chain resilience and production investment after 2022. Yet greater institutional density does not mean that interdependence has become symmetrical. While the official political-relations page emphasizes strategic cooperation and high-level contacts, the economic series shows a persistent deficit (Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye, n.d.-a, n.d.-b). This difference constitutes the central analytical tension of the 55-year relationship.

sections.title: Power Transition and Geoeconomic Connectivity: The Belt and Road Initiative and the Middle Corridor
paragraphs: China’s rise over the past quarter century rests on an accumulation of capacity that is not limited to the scale of production. Advanced manufacturing, energy and digital infrastructure, research and development, logistics, and development finance have increased China’s weight in international economic networks. Although this transformation gives China greater scope to influence regional rules and connections, it does not mean that all outcomes are determined unilaterally by Beijing. China’s rise proceeds through the interaction of identity, interdependence, and regional strategy, while partner countries’ regulatory capacities and national priorities substantially shape outcomes (Liu, 2010; Rolland, 2017).

Launched in 2013, the BRI is a multidimensional policy framework encompassing ports, energy networks, finance, digital connections, and cross-border production relations in addition to land and maritime transport routes. Official discourse surrounding the initiative emphasizes common development and mutual benefit; analytically, however, outcomes vary according to project selection, debt sustainability, procurement transparency, local employment, environmental impacts, and production linkages. The World Bank (2019) emphasizes that lower transport costs can create gains in trade and income, but that these gains will not be distributed equally without complementary reforms and risk management. The BRI should therefore be reduced neither to an infrastructure project nor presented as a model that automatically produces inclusive development.

Türkiye’s Middle Corridor vision refers to a multimodal network through which freight originating in China and Central Asia reaches Europe via the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Türkiye. The Baku-Tbilisi-Kars Railway, Marmaray, and railway and port connections in Türkiye are important components of this network. The corridor offers a complementary diversification option to the northern route through Russia and to maritime transport. Yet sea crossings, differing rail gauges, port transshipments, border waiting times, tariff predictability, and incompatibilities in digital documentation increase transport time and cost. Geographic shortness therefore does not automatically translate into operational superiority (Hussain, 2021; Ülgen & Umarov, 2024).

The World Bank’s (2023) model projects that, if the necessary infrastructure investments and efficiency measures are implemented, freight along the trans-Caspian Middle Corridor could almost triple from its 2021 level to reach 11 million tonnes by 2030, while travel time could be halved. The same report states that, without these improvements, demand would remain 35 percent below that projection. More importantly, China-Europe trade passing through the Caspian by 2030 is expected to account for only around 1 percent of total China-EU trade. This finding shows that the corridor is valuable primarily for regional trade and supply-chain diversification rather than as a single route that could replace global maritime transport.

Concrete investment in physical capacity is important for eliminating bottlenecks on the Türkiye section of the corridor. In December 2024 the World Bank approved USD 660 million in financing for the Eastern Türkiye Middle Corridor Railway Development Project. The project aims to electrify and modernize the 660-kilometer line between Divriği, Kars, and the Georgian border and has the potential to raise annual freight capacity from approximately 750,000 tonnes to 20 million tonnes (World Bank, 2024). The approved financing amounts to USD 660 million. Planned capacity, however, is not realized traffic volume; if border crossings, Caspian ports, and neighboring countries’ infrastructure are not improved simultaneously, investment in a single line will not raise corridor performance to the expected degree.

Strategic alignment between the BRI and the Middle Corridor therefore depends on three conditions. First, infrastructure investment must be complemented by common operating standards for customs, tariffs, data sharing, and timetables. Second, higher transit volumes must generate value-added services in Türkiye such as warehousing, maintenance, insurance, finance, and digital logistics. Third, manufacturing and export clusters should be established around the corridor so that logistics flows are connected to local production. If these conditions are not met, Türkiye’s geoeconomic importance may rise while its economic return remains confined to transit fees and limited logistics services.

In evaluating the corridor, the narrative of a “China-Europe land bridge” must also be distinguished from its regional-development function. In the World Bank model, most future volume is expected to originate not from China-Europe transit but from regional trade among Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Türkiye, and Europe (World Bank, 2023). This is not a weakness from Türkiye’s perspective; rather, it demonstrates that measuring the corridor’s success solely by the number of China-Europe containers is too narrow. Türkiye’s principal gains may arise through access by Anatolian production centers to Caucasian and Central Asian markets, logistics and processing activities in eastern provinces, port-rail integration, and the capacity to generate return freight. Since insufficient return freight increases empty wagon and container movements and erodes cost advantages, export diversification is also a corridor policy.

sections.title: Structural Asymmetries and the Transition from Transit Country to Joint Production Hub
paragraphs: The principal problem in Türkiye-China economic relations is not the size of trade volume so much as its imbalance and product composition. According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye (n.d.-a), in 2023 Türkiye exported USD 3.3 billion to China, imported USD 44.98 billion, recorded total trade of USD 48.3 billion, and ran a trade deficit of USD 41.7 billion. In 2025 exports remained at approximately USD 3.3 billion while imports rose to USD 49.6 billion and the deficit to USD 46.3 billion. The export-import coverage ratio in 2023 was only about 7.3 percent. This persistent gap points to a structural asymmetry that cannot be explained by temporary exchange-rate movements.

The product composition makes the technological dimension of the asymmetry visible. Türkiye’s principal exports to China include marble and travertine, metal ores, chromium, copper, iron, zinc, and boron products. Imports from China are led by telephones, automatic data-processing machines, electronic communications equipment, compressors, and converters (Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye, n.d.-a). In Yılmaz’s (2022) calculation based on International Trade Centre data, electrical machinery and equipment (SITC 85) together with machinery and mechanical appliances (SITC 84) accounted for 51.6 percent of total imports from China in 2018-2020. Türkiye’s exports, by contrast, were concentrated in natural resources and products at lower levels of processing. The deficit therefore reflects not only a monetary imbalance but also a qualitative difference in technological specialization.

Some of the machinery, electronic components, and capital goods imported from China are used as inputs in production processes in Türkiye. It would therefore be incorrect to interpret all imports as final consumption or as a “loss of domestic production.” The critical question is how much local value added, export capacity, and technological learning imported inputs generate in Türkiye. Open bilateral and firm-level data do not regularly show this linkage. Policy assessment therefore requires a framework that measures the contribution of intermediate and capital goods to local design, engineering, supplier development, and export capacity rather than simply setting a target of reducing imports.

Foreign direct investment data also demonstrate the difference between trade volume and production integration. According to Ülgen and Umarov (2024), the stock of Chinese foreign direct investment reached approximately USD 9 billion by the end of 2023. A total of 1,197 Chinese-capital companies have been established in Türkiye since 2002, representing around 0.6 percent of internationally financed companies in the country. Although Chinese investment is visible in strategic fields such as finance, energy, telecommunications, port operations, and infrastructure, export-oriented manufacturing investment remains insufficient in scale to offset the large trade deficit. Investment stock alone, moreover, should not be assumed to demonstrate technology transfer or local value added.

The approximately USD 1 billion investment agreement signed with BYD in July 2024 is an important test case for the transition from a transit function to a production function. According to the announcement, plans call for an electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle plant in Manisa with an annual capacity of 150,000 vehicles, a sustainable mobility R&D center, and up to 5,000 direct jobs; production is targeted to begin by the end of 2026 (Investment Office of the Presidency of the Republic of Türkiye, 2024). These are announced contractual targets, however, not realized outputs. The investment’s effect on Türkiye as a joint production hub should be measured through the local-sourcing ratio, components and patents developed in Türkiye, R&D expenditure, skilled employment, export ratio, and Turkish firms’ participation in BYD’s global supply network.

Local value added and technology transfer should not be used interchangeably. Local value added refers to economic value created in Türkiye through wages, purchases of local inputs, taxes, logistics, and service activities. Technology transfer, by contrast, requires production knowledge, design capabilities, intellectual property, or advanced engineering practices to be transferred to institutions and employees in Türkiye. An assembly plant may create substantial employment and local service procurement while technology transfer remains limited if core components are imported and design decisions remain abroad. Conversely, a smaller R&D partnership can generate long-term technological effects through patents, licenses, or specialist training. Investment value, local value, and technological learning should therefore be monitored as separate indicators when assessing the joint-production-hub function.

Taken together, the indicators place Türkiye between a pure transit country and an institutionalized joint production hub, but in an intermediate position dominated by the transit function. Railway investment and the Middle Corridor’s growing visibility strengthen its logistics advantage. Persistent high trade deficits, the division between raw-material exports and technology-intensive imports, the relatively limited scale of production investment, and insufficient open data on realized technology transfer, however, show that joint-production-hub status has not yet been demonstrated. Geography is a necessary precondition, but it is not production transformation itself.

The first axis of possible solutions is exports and market access. Türkiye’s exports to China should be diversified toward higher-value-added fields such as processed minerals, machinery and automotive components, medical technology, chemicals, food, and digital services. Compliance with health and technical standards in the Chinese market, product-specific protocols for agricultural and food products, e-commerce channels, and distribution partnerships can support this objective. Success should be monitored not only through total export value but also by the number of new products, the share of processed goods, services exports, and durable market access.

The second axis is the quality of investment. Incentives should be tied not only to the amount of capital invested but also to indicators such as the local-sourcing ratio, R&D expenditure, skilled employment, joint patents, engineering training, export capacity, and environmental performance. Joint ventures and supplier-development programs can facilitate Turkish firms’ participation in Chinese companies’ global value chains. If public support is graduated according to realized production and technology outputs rather than announced capacity, the gap between investment volume and development impact can be reduced.

The third axis is data and institutional monitoring capacity. An annual “economic partnership performance framework” could be published under the Türkiye-China Joint Working Group. It should monitor the trade balance, technological intensity of products, share of greenfield investment, local sourcing, joint R&D and patents, skilled employment, exports to third countries, and the corridor’s time-cost performance. Aggregated indicators that protect firms’ confidential information would allow investment agreements to be evaluated in terms of public benefit and reciprocity.

sections.title: Türkiye’s Strategic Balancing Role and Its Limits
paragraphs: Türkiye’s role in Eurasia derives from the combination of geographic location, institutional ties, and diplomatic capacity. Its position at the intersection of the Balkans, the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Middle East, and the Eastern Mediterranean, together with its NATO membership, Customs Union with the EU, role in the Organization of Turkic States, and responsibilities in Black Sea security, enables Türkiye to engage simultaneously with different centers of power. These characteristics do not make Türkiye the “sole” actor capable of ensuring stability during Eurasia’s power transition. More cautiously, Türkiye can be regarded as one of several actors capable of making a limited but important contribution through transport, crisis diplomacy, and regional networks.

The first limit on this balancing capacity is U.S.-China strategic competition. Advanced technology, telecommunications, semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and critical-infrastructure investment are increasingly treated as matters of security policy. Türkiye’s NATO commitments and regulatory integration with the EU market can create constraints on technology cooperation with China in areas such as data security, export controls, competition, and standards compliance. Conversely, treating all Chinese investment as a security threat could also restrict opportunities in production and the green transition. A workable strategy therefore requires sector-based risk assessment, supply diversification, and transparent investment screening rather than a claim of equal distance from all actors (Tekdal, 2023; Ülgen & Umarov, 2024).

The second limit is the social and political importance of the Uyghur issue in Türkiye. The Uyghur diaspora in Türkiye, cultural and historical ties, and human-rights debates make it difficult to isolate Ankara-Beijing relations completely from other economic issues. A persistent difference exists between Beijing’s emphasis on sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs and societal sensitivities in Türkiye. Ignoring this area will not build trust in the relationship; high-level dialogue, consular access, open communication on cultural and religious rights, and protection of the diaspora’s security are necessary to keep the disagreement manageable (Öniş & Yalikun, 2021; Ülgen & Umarov, 2024).

The third limit is the potential transformation of economic networks into instruments of pressure. Dependence on a single supplier at critical telecommunications, financial, energy, or transport nodes can give the actor at the center of the network disproportionate informational and access power (Farrell & Newman, 2019). For Türkiye, the trade deficit and dependence on China for certain technology inputs require balancing short-term cost advantages against long-term resilience. Open procurement, cybersecurity auditing, interoperable standards, source diversification, and dispute-settlement provisions in contracts can reduce this risk. Strategic balancing should mean measuring and managing dependencies rather than denying them.

The economic sustainability of Türkiye’s balancing role also depends on whether its Western and Asian connections are constructed as mutually exclusive alternatives. Europe remains Türkiye’s largest export market and regulatory reference point, while China is important for technology, capital goods, finance, and access to Asian markets. Pursuing both orientations together requires Chinese investment to comply with EU competition, environmental, and product-safety standards; goods produced in Türkiye to meet Customs Union rules; and security consultations with allies in sensitive technologies. Successful balancing will arise not from obscuring institutional commitments, but from coordinating cooperation with different partners around clear rules and national industrial objectives.

sections.title: A New Peace Perspective and Sustainable Cooperation
paragraphs: In this study, the “new peace perspective” is used not as an established independent theory in the international-relations literature but as an integrative analytical framework developed to evaluate Türkiye-China relations. The concept does not limit peace to the absence of armed conflict between states; it considers together the contributions of balanced economic interdependence, sustainable development, institutionalized connectivity, and uninterrupted diplomatic dialogue to predictability. This approach draws on Galtung’s (1969) distinction between negative and positive peace, Keohane and Nye’s (2012) framework of complex interdependence, and debates on commercial peace.

According to the commercial-peace approach, deeper economic relations can raise the opportunity cost of conflict and diplomatic rupture. Oneal and Russett (1997) provide findings indicating that mutual trade may reduce the probability of interstate military conflict. This result is not unconditional, however. Barbieri (1996) shows that intense dependence can increase the risk of disputes when the nature and symmetry of economic ties are not taken into account. In Copeland’s (1996) trade-expectations approach, the decisive factor is not only current trade volume but expectations about whether mutually beneficial trade will continue in the future. Farrell and Newman (2019), meanwhile, show that asymmetric networks can be used for sanctions, surveillance, and restrictions on access.

The causal mechanism of the new peace perspective consists of four linkages. First, balanced trade, reciprocal investment, and joint production raise the cost of political rupture for both sides. Second, transport and production networks increase the number of firms, employees, local governments, and expert communities that benefit from continuation of the relationship. Third, joint working groups, data sharing, and dispute-resolution mechanisms reduce misperception and uncertainty. Fourth, mediation and crisis diplomacy keep channels of communication open during periods of political disagreement. Connectivity contributes to stability only through these institutional and diplomatic intermediary mechanisms.

The boundary conditions of the mechanism are symmetry, institutionalization, diversification, and positive expectations about the future. If the trade deficit continuously expands, one-sided dependence on critical inputs deepens, investment fails to generate local benefits, security dilemmas intensify, or economic networks are used for political pressure, more connectivity may not produce more peace. The USD 41.7 billion 2023 deficit in Türkiye-China relations and the technology-intensive structure of imports directly concern this boundary condition. The new peace perspective is therefore not a deterministic proposition that “trade guarantees peace,” but a conditional proposition that interdependence managed through balanced and reliable institutions can reduce the risk of conflict.

China’s Global Development, Global Security, and Global Civilization initiatives present an official global-governance discourse combining emphases on development, sovereignty, dialogue, and cultural diversity. The Global Civilization Initiative was announced in 2023 around principles including respect for the diversity of civilizations, mutual learning, and people-to-people exchange (Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the People’s Republic of China, 2023). These documents indicate Beijing’s policy preferences and legitimacy discourse; they are not independent empirical evidence that the initiatives produce peace in practice. Their significance for Türkiye-China relations depends on whether concrete investment and diplomatic mechanisms can be tested against criteria of reciprocity and transparency.

Türkiye’s complementary contribution lies in its capacity for mediation and facilitation. Following the “Mediation for Peace” initiative launched by Türkiye and Finland within the United Nations in 2010, a Group of Friends of Mediation was established, and Türkiye has hosted the Istanbul Mediation Conferences since 2012 (Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye, 2022). During the Russia-Ukraine War, talks in Antalya and Istanbul and the Black Sea Grain Initiative launched on July 22, 2022 demonstrated Ankara’s ability to open limited and functional areas of cooperation among the parties. The Joint Coordination Centre in Istanbul brought together representatives of Russia, Ukraine, Türkiye, and the United Nations (United Nations, 2022). These initiatives did not end the war; they temporarily facilitated communication and the provision of specific public goods.

The Türkiye-China linkage is clear at this point, but conditional. If alignment between the BRI and the Middle Corridor produces joint production, local sourcing, and predictable transport, the number of actors benefiting from continuation of the relationship will increase. Regular economic consultations, crisis communication, customs and data standards, resolution of investment disputes, and inter-university research networks can reduce uncertainty. Conversely, if trade asymmetry deepens, the Uyghur issue remains a suppressed tension, or technology networks generate one-sided pressure, connectivity may create vulnerability rather than stability. The contribution of the new peace perspective to bilateral relations depends on combining China’s investment and production capacity with Türkiye’s connectivity and diplomacy instruments in a balanced, measurable, and institutionalized partnership.

For the framework to be monitored empirically, claims about peace and stability must be tied to measurable intermediate outcomes. The continuation of regular high-level and technical meetings, resolution of trade disputes through predictable mechanisms, operation of joint crisis protocols during corridor disruptions, more balanced distribution of economic benefits, and keeping communication channels open despite political disagreements are positive indicators. Sudden trade restrictions, unilateral imposition of standards, linking access to critical networks to political conditions, investments that fail to generate local benefits, and societal sensitivities interrupting diplomatic communication are signs of failure. These observable outcomes turn the concept of “new peace” from a normative aspiration into a set of analytically testable propositions.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study evaluates the stage reached in Türkiye-China relations on the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations through the distinction between a “transit country” and a “joint production hub.” The clear answer to the research question is that Türkiye currently occupies an intermediate position dominated by its transit function. The Middle Corridor and railway investment in Türkiye are increasing the country’s logistical importance; geographic location and transport capacity alone, however, do not constitute a joint production hub. Such a transformation requires China-origin investment to generate local sourcing, joint R&D, realized technology transfer, skilled employment, and exports to third countries.

The main findings support this conclusion in three respects. First, exports of USD 3.3 billion against imports of USD 44.98 billion and a deficit of USD 41.7 billion in 2023 demonstrate the pronounced trade asymmetry in the relationship. Second, machinery and electrical-equipment groups accounted for 51.6 percent of imports from China in 2018-2020, revealing a difference in technological specialization when considered together with Türkiye’s raw-material-heavy exports. Third, although the approximately USD 9 billion stock of Chinese investment at the end of 2023 and BYD’s production-R&D plan point to transition potential, realized local value added and technology outputs do not yet substantiate the claim that Türkiye is a joint production hub. The World Bank’s projection of 11 million tonnes for the Middle Corridor in 2030 is likewise a conditional regional opportunity; the expected share of roughly 1 percent of China-EU trade demonstrates the corridor’s limits.

The article’s theoretical contribution is to combine power transition and geoeconomic connectivity through production indicators and a conditional peace mechanism. The new peace perspective does not treat trade and infrastructure as factors that automatically produce peace; it defines balanced distribution of economic benefits, positive expectations about future cooperation, institutional dispute resolution, and supply diversification as necessary conditions. At the policy level, annual performance indicators, local-sourcing and R&D conditions in investment incentives, customs-digitalization harmonization, and transparent management of technology risks should be prioritized. The green transition, electric mobility, renewable energy, the digital economy, and university-industry cooperation are among the main fields capable of transforming logistical proximity into production partnership.

The study’s limitations arise from irregular firm-level data on local value added, joint patents, technology transfer, and investment performance, as well as from the fact that the 2030 corridor figures are model projections rather than realized data. Document analysis identifies mechanisms and indicator patterns within the relationship but does not measure the magnitude of causal effects. Future research should compare local sourcing, R&D, and export effects using TurkStat microdata, UN Comtrade product-level series, firm surveys, and case studies of Chinese investment in Türkiye. Once such data are available, it will be possible to test more precisely over time whether Türkiye is moving from a transit-dominant intermediate position toward a joint production hub. Such monitoring will also make it possible to evaluate at regular intervals whether the relationship after its 55th year moves from discourse to measurable production outcomes.
